summary:
SILENT SENTINELS :
Under the theme "Abandoned but Not Forgotten",  we have developed a website dedicated to preserving the stories and scientific contributions of space exploration missions to Mars, the Moon, and deep space. The platform brings together information about rovers, landers, and other special missions, exploring their purpose, design, journey, discoveries, operational lifespan, current status, and the scientific knowledge they have contributed.

Using information and images from official NASA sources, the website presents each mission through detailed profiles, visual timelines, maps, and other engaging features. It aims to help students and space enthusiasts discover the remarkable journeys of these machines and understand the importance of their contributions to space exploration.

Although many of these missions have completed their journeys or fallen silent, their discoveries continue to shape our understanding of the universe. Through this platform, we ensure that their stories, achievements, and scientific legacies are never forgotten.
Project link- https://silent-sentinels.vercel.app/
details:
Project Name: Silent Sentinels

Project link- https://silent-sentinels.vercel.app/

1. What does it do and how does it work?

We built Silent Sentinels to bring NASA’s most famous space probes to life for students and space enthusiasts (especially teenagers aged 14 to 19). Instead of just reading boring Wikipedia articles or textbooks, users can explore real NASA spacecraft in full 3D right in their web browser.

Here’s what you can do on the site:

Spin and inspect 3D spacecraft: You can rotate and zoom into realistic 3D models of probes like Voyager 1, Pioneer 10, New Horizons, and Cassini. Clicking on glowing hotspots shows how each part works—like nuclear batteries and giant dish antennas.

Explore 3D Moon and Mars globes: You can spin 3D globes of the Moon and Mars to see exactly where historical NASA missions and rovers landed.

Solve real space challenges: We added interactive mini-games where you calculate how long radio signals take to travel billions of kilometers across space at the speed of light.

Earn mission badges: As you explore missions and solve challenges, you unlock badges in your personal locker to keep track of what you’ve learned.

Real NASA data: Every distance, launch date, and mission fact comes directly from NASA’s official scientific records (NSSDCA).

2. What benefits does it have?

Makes learning fun: Most space websites are walls of text. We turn space science into a visual, interactive experience that feels like playing a video game.

Helps physics make sense: When students see how far Voyager is and calculate the delay in radio signals themselves, concepts like the speed of light and radio waves click instantly.

Runs on anything: You don't need to download or install anything, and you don't need an expensive gaming computer. It works smoothly right in Google Chrome or Edge on ordinary laptops and phones.

3. What is the intended impact?

We want to inspire high school and college students to get genuinely excited about space exploration, astrophysics, and engineering. Many young people don't know that probes launched decades ago are still flying in deep space right now. We want to celebrate these robotic "sentinels" and maybe inspire someone using our site to become NASA’s next aerospace engineer.

4. What tools, coding languages, and software did you use?

Frontend: React, TypeScript, and Vite for building the web app fast.

3D Graphics: Three.js and WebGL to render the 3D spacecraft models, planets, and starry backgrounds.

Styling: Tailwind CSS to design the dark-mode cosmic theme.

Database & Login: Supabase (PostgreSQL) to store user accounts, challenge scores, and unlocked badges safely.

AI Tools: We used Google Gemini / Antigravity as a coding helper to write and debug code and create realistic cosmic background art.

Hosting & Code: Git, GitHub Desktop, GitHub for version control, and Vercel to deploy the website live on the internet.

5. How is your project creative?

Instead of making a typical educational website that feels like homework, we designed Silent Sentinels to feel like sitting inside a futuristic mission control center. We combined cinematic cosmic visuals (like glowing nebulae and black holes) with gamified learning—you don't just read about the missions, you take on challenges, decode secret messages, and earn astronaut-style badges.

6. What factors did our team consider?

Keeping it interesting for teens: We knew 14–19 year olds get bored quickly with long articles, so we kept text bite-sized and focused on 3D interaction and mini-games.

Scientific accuracy: We made sure not to make up fake numbers. All speeds, coordinates, and distances were cross-checked with real NASA data.

Making it run without lag: 3D graphics can easily slow down a computer. We spent a lot of time optimizing our 3D code (capping resolution and pausing scenes when scrolled out of view) so it runs smoothly at 60 FPS even on school laptops.

Safety and privacy: We used secure database rules in Supabase so user accounts and passwords are safe.
